lede: The pull request is not a quality control. It is a queue. Once the author is a machine that can be checked mechanically before the merge, the queue is the slowest element in the pipeline and the diff-reading human is its weakest check. This article describes how one agent-first delivery system removed the pull request without removing the checks, what had to replace it, and what that has cost so far.

p: Throughput against attention. A fleet of coding agents produces verified changes faster than any reviewer can read them; every hour a card waits for a human, the queue behind it grows and the next human decision gets coarser.

Accountability against speed. Removing the review step is easy; removing the record, the segregation of duties and the norm-keeping that came with it is not. If nothing takes those functions over, the codebase drifts while every gate stays green.

Honesty of status against convenience. A board that lets a card reach 'done' on a lane move, a pipeline success flag or an agent's closing sentence will eventually show delivered work that is not on the integration branch. Without a human reading every diff, completion has to be a claim the platform can verify.

Independence of checks against correlated errors. A reviewer model that shares lineage, prompt or context with the author model confirms more than it finds. Deterministic checks that need no model at all have to stay in the path.
Policy against practice. Some repositories answer to a rule that demands a named human approver. The pattern has to degrade into a verified pull request rather than into an unreviewed merge.

Agent Studio, the delivery system behind this article, opens zero pull requests for its own development. Its board, task server, runners and review pipeline are open source, and the mechanics below are taken from its documentation and code rather than from a target picture.

The platform owns git. A run agent edits files in a worktree and does not branch, stage, commit, push or merge (ADR-0052). The pipeline commits the run's changes, attributes them to the card's run windows and, for remote runners, publishes the result as an immutable, fenced delivery ref named refs/heads/agent-studio/results/<attempt>/fence-<n>/<sha>. The ref carries a fencing token minted with the run's lease, so a superseded attempt cannot republish under a newer one's identity. Review and delivery writes go through an attempt-authority store; a stale fence is answered with StaleFence, an expired lease with LeaseExpired, and the write is dropped.

Gates sit in front of the merge. A build-and-test gate runs the suite against the current integration head and is fail-closed: the review outcome must be Pass and the build/test aspect must pass or belong to the explicit not-applicable class. Named review aspects return Pass, Concerns or Block with findings; a separate code-review grade from A to D is stored as reporting evidence and, by decision, is never a lane gate. A failed completion, evidence or solution-quality check reissues the card with findings; the budget is two automatic reissues per card, after which the card escalates to a human and is never accepted by default.

Integration happens before human review. A green delivery is merged into the integration branch before the card reaches the Human Review lane; the lane then shows verdicts, evidence and the computed integration state, and a diff is opened only when something is contested. Release is a separate event: develop to main is a manual promotion with its own test gate, and a stable freeze is a third, explicit act. The system's own release page insists these four events are not conflated.

Completion is a claim that requires proof. The card's integration record is recomputed from git ancestry of its attributed commits and takes one of five values: integrated, partial, pending, conflict-skipped or no-branch. Lane, pipeline success and prose cannot force 'integrated'. Since card AGT-2543 no card reaches Completed while its delivery is not integrated; the only exception is an operator override that must be set explicitly on the move and is recorded with its reason. A merge that fails on a textual conflict leaves the card visibly conflict-skipped with the conflicted files in the verdict and offers Rebase & retry; content rescued from a dying run goes to a salvage ref that stays outside the review subject until someone adopts it; a completion claimed outside the runner is re-verified by the server against the repository and, if it cannot be proven, becomes an unverified-delivery record instead of a weaker stamp.

p: The human's unit of work changes from 'read this diff' to 'sight this verdict stream'. Operators spot-check a sample, open a diff when a verdict is contested or the blast radius is large, and spend the rest of their attention on shaping tasks and deciding on findings. Oversight moves to the altitude where a person can still be useful for more than one change every ten minutes.

The audit trail improves rather than disappears, provided it is re-homed. Task history, attributed commits, fenced refs, review reports and the integration record are platform-owned and not writable by the delivering agent, which is a stronger record than an approval click on a pull request. Knowledge transfer and norms, the part of code review that Google's study found most valuable, have to be carried by specs, decision records and living documentation.

Status becomes checkable. Because 'done' is derived from git ancestry, the board can be wrong only in ways the platform can name: conflict-skipped, no-branch, a stale attribution. Those failures are visible and repairable; a human's silent misreading of a large diff was neither.

Gate configuration becomes a protected surface. When a gate blocks under delivery pressure, the cheapest local fix is to weaken it. Review standards, gate profiles and override rules therefore need their own change history and their own reviewer, and the override must be loud.

Compute replaces attention, and compute has a queue too. Every delivery now runs a full suite and a review pass; when the fleet runs hot, the review lane fills faster than it drains. The cost section below quantifies this.

When the gate layer does not exist yet. Without a deterministic gate that can block a merge on its own, and a review verdict with a defined shape, removing the human gate converts a review bottleneck into a change-failure problem that is slower to notice. Build the gates first; keep the pull request until they have blocked something real.

When an external rule demands a named human approver. Keep the pull request and run the gates in front of it. Agent Studio itself keeps a configured pull-request integration strategy for that case: a delivery marked for pull-request handoff stays in Human Review and is never reported as merged.

When change volume is low. A small team with a short review queue has no bottleneck to remove; a fast human pull request is cheaper than building and maintaining gate, verdict and integration-record infrastructure.

When author and reviewer are the same model family with the same prompts and context. Three green verdicts are then worth little more than one. Rotate models and prompts, keep checks that need no model, and keep a sampled human audit before trusting the verdict stream alone.

Bounce rounds. The platform's own cycle-time reading for its last 30 days (416 tasks, taken on 2026-08-23) counts 5,842 lane moves, 1,187 of them backwards across 259 tasks. Operator requeues (354 moves, median rework 1.9 hours, 95 days of rework time in total) and escalation requeues (187 moves, 52 days) leak the most time; build/test gate failures (112, median rework 10 minutes) and quality-loop reopens (163, 12 minutes) are frequent but cheap. The gates do their job quickly; the expensive loops are the ones that end at a human.

The full suite per delivery. In the same system's seven-day reading the build/test gate takes a median of 2.1 hours per delivery and is the largest compute-bound stage, while the wait for post-processing runs at 1.2 days and human review at 2.1 days, against a lead time of 3.8 days. When the coding fleet runs hot, the review lane's inflow is roughly twice its outflow. That is why a batch gate, which would run one full suite for a wave of fenced, reviewed deliveries and bisect on failure, exists as a decision-pending dossier. It is a documented proposal, not a shipped feature, and the pattern does not depend on it; it is the price of running every gate per card.

Status that lied before it was made verifiable. The acceptance invariant was written after a series of incidents, not before: cards stamped Delivered from prose that nothing re-checked against git, and a bulk acceptance of 35 remote-runner cards on 2026-07-24 and 2026-07-28 in which every sampled merge step reported no-branch because the merge runner looked for a branch name the remote runner had not published. The integration record, the attributed-commit ancestry check and the explicit operator override are the repairs. They cost several weeks of attention.

Known open edges. The system's own adversarial review of its status model lists git as an unfenced side channel: a superseded runner generation can still push to the same card ref that the winning generation delivers on, and commit attribution can lose or misattribute commits across generations. Both are documented weaknesses with cards behind them, not solved guarantees. The pattern works because these gaps are named and visible; it would not work if they were assumed away.

The verdict stream is only legible if the decisions behind the gates are kept current. Which aspects block, which overrides are legitimate and why a card was requeued are memory, and memory decays. The companion article, Memory Management Is the New Code, is about that layer.
